{"id": "51585f0c-e83a-4a63-b258-0bf5c178eb3c", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_1y8dAXh4nzUkkIIQ8ff3Af", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"DevOps Agent IAM permissions\",\"context\":\"# DevOps Agent IAM permissions\\n\\nAWS DevOps Agent uses service-specific AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) actions to control access to its features and capabilities. These actions determine what users can do within the AWS DevOps Agent console and Operator Web App. This is separate from the AWS service API permissions that the agent itself uses to investigate your resources.\\n\\nFor more information about limiting agent access, see Limiting Agent Access in an AWS Account.\\n\\nTo let the agent perform directed actions in your AWS accounts, register an elevated IAM role on the account association. For example, you might use an elevated role to remediate an issue after operator approval. For more information about directed actions and registering an elevated IAM role, see Working with directed actions\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/devopsagent/latest/userguide/aws-devops-agent-security-devops-agent-iam-permissions.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Permissions for AWS DevOps Agent\",\"context\":\"# Permissions for AWS DevOps Agent\\n\\nIf you set up AWS DevOps Agent for the **Operate** capabilities, your identity needs two kinds of permissions: read access so the IDE extension can show status, and permissions to create the access role and Agent Space.\\n\\nTo show the Agent Space status and its integrations, the IDE extension uses AWS DevOps Agent read permissions, including `aidevops:ListServices` and `aidevops:ListAssociations`.\\n\\nSetting up AWS DevOps Agent requires permission to create an IAM role and an Agent Space. Your coding agent checks your permissions before setup. If anything is missing, it tells you what\u2019s needed and gives you a note to send to your AWS administrator. For the permissions AWS DevOps Agent uses, see DevOps Agent IAM permissions in the *AWS DevOps Agent User Guide*.\\n\\nThe access role trusts only the Agent Space in your account. Setup does not attach `AIDevOpsAgentActionsPolicy` and does not create an elevated role, so AWS DevOps Agent recommends fixes but does not apply them. AWS DevOps Agent actions are logged in AWS CloudTrail. To remove AWS DevOps Agent, delete the access role or the Agent Space. For more information about how AWS DevOps Agent uses IAM roles and Agent Spaces, see the AWS DevOps Agent User Guide\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/startupadvisor/latest/userguide/security-iam-devops-agent.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Getting started with AWS DevOps Agent using Terraform\",\"context\":\"## Troubleshooting\\n\\n**IAM propagation delays**\\n\\n* The configuration includes a 30-second `time_sleep` between IAM role creation and Agent Space creation. The DevOps Agent service validates the operator role's trust policy during Agent Space creation, and this can fail if IAM hasn't fully propagated. If you still see trust policy errors, wait a minute and run `terraform apply` again \u2014 the IAM roles will already exist and the apply will pick up where it left off.\\n\\n**ServiceNow `instanceId does not match` error**\\n\\n* Set `instance_id` explicitly in the `service_now` integration block to the short instance name (for example, `\\\"ven04972\\\"`), not the full `instance_url`. See the note in Part 3 above.\\n\\n**Dynatrace association `status: invalid`**\\n\\n* If `terraform apply` succeeds but the resulting association reports `status = \\\"invalid\\\"` (visible using `aws devops-agent get-association` or the console), this indicates Dynatrace rejected the OAuth client credentials. Double-check `client_id`, `client_secret`, and `account_urn` against the Dynatrace account, rather than a Terraform configuration issue.\\n\\n**Permission errors**\\n\\n* Verify that your AWS credentials have the necessary IAM permissions to create roles and policies.\\n* Check that the trust policy conditions match your account ID.\\n\\n**Cross-account deployment fails**\\n\\n* The `aws.service` provider must be configured with credentials for the service account. Use a named profile or an assume role block.\\n* Verify that the `agent_space_arn` value matches the ARN from the Part 1 output.\\n\\n**Terraform resource type not found**\\n\\n* Verify that you have the `awscc` provider version `~> 1.0` or later. The `awscc_devopsagent_agent_space` and `awscc_devopsagent_association` resources require the AWS Cloud Control provider.\\n* The `awscc_devopsagent_asset` and `awscc_devopsagent_trigger` resources used in Part 4 require `awscc` provider version 1.98.0 or later. Run `terraform providers` to check your version, and run `terraform init -upgrade` after raising the version constraint\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/devopsagent/latest/userguide/getting-started-with-aws-devops-agent-getting-started-with-aws-devops-agent-using-terraform.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS docs for stale Bedrock access check"}
